Header:
Date: 2025-01-28

Attendees: Jesse Alvarez (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Tom Reynolds (Velorum CTO); Maya Bennett (Platform Eng); Claire Zhou (Infra); Aaron Li (ML Eng)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jesse: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll do a deep dive today on autoscaling and capacity planning, especially how burst policies and queueing models interact with our reserved GPU offering. Priya will drive the tech bit.
[00:15] Priya: hi all, quick agenda: 1) current velorum infra and perf goals 2) autoscale patterns we see 3) queueing and burst policy options 4) KV cache / batching impact 5) on-prem / VPC notes. sound good?
[00:28] Tom: yes thanks. to head off, our primary constraint is p95 latency under 400ms for interactive flows, but we also have nightly large batch jobs. we see frequent spikes when scheduled reports start, and on marketing days there are 3x spikes.
[00:45] Maya: and data residency — all inference must remain in our VPC; we can't have request payloads leave our subnet. we will consider private deployment.
[01:02] Priya: ok good — that's exactly the combination where reserved GPUs + burst pools are useful. quick question — what's your average qps outside spikes?
[01:12] Aaron: baseline is 25 qps, typical 95th is 60 qps and spikes to 180 qps for ~10 minutes during report windows.
[01:25] Priya: thanks, that gives us a ballpark. architecturally, Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved GPU nodes sized for baseline load, and a configurable burst pool for short spikes. the burst pool can be pre-warmed or cold; warm burst nodes reduce cold-start latency but incur reservation costs.
[01:44] Tom: how do you handle queueing? We can't accept unbounded latency; we prefer some requests to fail fast rather than queue forever.
[01:52] Priya: yeah, we usually recommend a hybrid: token-level scheduling with per-request SLA buckets. requests marked interactive go to a high-priority low-latency lane with aggressive autoscale and pre-warm; batch/async jobs go to a lower priority queue with longer tail latency allowed. we also have a queue-depth-based admission policy — once queue length for the high-priority lane exceeds threshold, we return a 429 with retry-after or redirect to async.
[02:17] Claire: can you talk about the queueing model in more detail — is it FIFO? do you do priority preemption?
[02:25] Priya: by default it's priority queues with FIFO within priority. we support preemption for CPU-bound preprocessing (e.g., tokenization) but not mid-stream token generation preemption — we favor graceful degradation: redirect to a smaller model variant or to cached prefixes. that's where KV cache comes in.
[02:40] Jesse: also worth noting our smart routing can fallback to quantized models when capacity constrained — it depends on your quality guardrails.
[02:50] Tom: about KV cache — how do we warm it for expected traffic? if 180 qps hits, how much cache miss rate do you expect?
[02:59] Priya: good question — KV cache warmup depends on prefix reuse and session affinity. for chat-style workloads with repeated user context, warmup is quick; for many one-off prompts, it's cold. we can seed cache by pre-warming popular prompt families; Redwood has tooling to pre-populate KV entries for known conversational flows. Miss rates vary — we typically see 10–30% miss during first two minutes of a spike without pre-warm. with pre-warm it drops under 5% for targeted flows. note: warm KV cache reduces token generation latency because the model doesn't need to recompute earlier layers.
[03:40] Aaron: what about batching? our interactive latency target is tight — can we still batch?
[03:46] Priya: yes, batching is workload aware. continuous batching enables micro-batches for interactive flows (batch sizes 2–8) which preserves latency but improves throughput. For high throughput async jobs we use larger batch sizes. Redwood's runtime does dynamic batch formation and can cap per-request latency. there is a trade-off: for short sequences (<= 64 tokens) batching yields big efficiency gains; for long sequences batching benefits reduce.
[04:14] Maya: and quantization — we are concerned about hallucination/regression when using int8 or 4-bit quant. what's your recommendation?
[04:22] Priya: quantization can reduce memory and increase throughput, but there's a small quality delta. our recommended approach: run a quality eval set — Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per-model and per-workload. for critical flows, keep fp16; for non-critical, int8 or 4-bit with post-deployment monitoring and rollback.
[04:40] Tom: can you show the math for sizing reserved GPUs given our baseline/spike numbers?
[04:47] Priya: sure — quick back-of-envelope. assume your model consumes ~40 tokens/sec per GPU given sequence length and optimized kernels — actually let's do it in terms of concurrency: if a single A100-class GPU supports ~12 concurrent generation streams at p50 80ms per token for your model, then for baseline 60 qps you might need N GPUs = ceil(60 / (streams_per_gpu * throughput_per_stream)). but simpler: Redwood provides benchmark profiles per model; we map your p95 latency target and qps distribution to an SLO curve and recommend a commit for baseline plus a burst multiplier. 
[05:28] Jesse: i'll put a simple example in the follow-up doc. e.g., baseline 60 qps -> 4 GPUs reserved, burst pool sized to add 6 GPUs for short spikes to cover 180 qps. exact numbers depend on sequence lengths and quant.
[05:41] Claire: how fast can burst nodes come online from cold?
[05:45] Priya: cold provision can be minutes (3–6) depending on infra and image pull; warm burst nodes are kept idle but available with sub-30s readiness. there's also a middle ground — keep smaller hot pool. warm pools cost more but keep p95 for spikes.
[06:00] Tom: what's Redwood's pricing model for reserved vs burst? are warm nodes billed as reserved?
[06:07] Jesse: reserved nodes are part of your commit. warm burst nodes can be part of an optional pre-warm add-on billed at a reduced standby rate; cold bursts are billed on usage. we'll share exact tiered pricing in the doc.
[06:18] Aaron: network-wise for VPC/on-prem, do you support direct peering and private control plane?
[06:24] Priya: yes — Private deployment offers a customer-managed control plane inside VPC and the inference plane on your subnets. we support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and on-prem air-gapped package. audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO/SAML are available.
[06:38] Maya: what about autoscaler policy — are we limited to simple CPU-based autoscale? we prefer token-rate based autoscaling.
[06:45] Priya: Redwood autoscaler uses a mix of signals: queue depth, token production rate, GPU utilization, and p95 tail latency. token-rate based scaling is the primary signal for model-serving autoscale; queue-length is used for admission control. this avoids noisy scaling from transient CPU spikes.
[07:02] Tom: is there hysteresis to avoid flapping with short spikes?
[07:06] Priya: yes we have cooldown windows and exponential backoff for scale-down. plus cost-aware policies: minimum commit fraction for Dedicated and optional scale-down throttles.
[07:16] Claire: can we throttle certain customer segments during spikes? we have premium users who need priority.
[07:22] Priya: absolutely — routing and tenant-level priority are supported. you can set per-tenant SLA buckets that map to queues and auto-scale policies.
[07:30] Aaron: curious about cold-start of KV cache and model weights — on on-prem what's the image size / warm time?
[07:36] Priya: model weights with fp16 for a 70B model are several tens of GB; with 4-bit it's smaller. cold load includes pulling weights into GPU memory and loading NVMe cache; this is the main contributor to minutes-level startup. to mitigate, we recommend either keeping a small warm pool or leveraging local disk cache on nodes and pre-placed artifacts.
[07:58] Jesse: we also provide an image that can be pre-provisioned in your air-gapped registry for on-prem.
[08:03] Tom: for queue admission, do you support priority decay? like demote long-running requests to lower priority?
[08:10] Priya: we support priority aging and tiered timeouts: requests that exceed X seconds can be downgraded or completed with partial output depending on your policy. important for long generation tasks.
[08:22] Maya: operationally, what metrics should we track for capacity planning?
[08:27] Priya: recommend: qps breakdown by route, p50/p95/p99 token latency, queue depth per-priority, KV cache hit/miss, GPU utilization, model load times, and token throughput per-GPU. Redwood Console provides these dashboards and export.
[08:41] Tom: how do you estimate cost impact of changing batching/quantization? we need to run internal cost models.
[08:47] Priya: Redwood Optimize can simulate cost curves: input your workload histogram and it recommends batching config and quant profiles with estimated cost and predicted latency impact. we can run a pilot and provide per-token cost delta numbers.
[09:00] Aaron: any gotchas for stateful workloads with KV cache in multi-tenant cluster? eviction and mem isolation?
[09:07] Priya: KV cache is namespace-scoped. on Dedicated you get per-customer KV partitions. eviction is LRU with TTLs and we expose metrics for per-tenant cache pressure. memory isolation strategies prevent noisy neighbor cache evictions.
[09:23] Claire: what about failover if a reserved node dies during a spike?
[09:27] Priya: we have automatic reroute to burst pool or fallback model variants. for critical traffic we recommend multi-az placement for reserved capacity. failover is transparent but may increase latency briefly.
[09:39] Tom: can we run a short benchmark today? even a synthetic run to validate baseline numbers?
[09:44] Jesse: we can agree to a bench. practical approach: you send 1) representative prompt set 2) traffic histogram and 3) sequence length distribution. we'll run a dedicated cluster run and return p95/p99 numbers.
[09:58] Maya: for the bench, we need to verify VPC-only network path — do you support running bench in our VPC?
[10:05] Priya: yes, we can run a benchmark within your VPC for private deployment; on hosted we can replicate network characteristics but for real validation we prefer private bench.
[10:14] Aaron: about metrics retention and logging — we need audit-level logs for compliance.
[10:19] Priya: we support audit logs, full request/response hashes (configurable), and integration with your SIEM via Kinesis/Cloudwatch or SFTP. retention tiers are available as add-ons.
[10:31] Tom: any experience with reserving GPUs for nightly batch jobs to avoid interfering with interactive flows?
[10:37] Priya: yes — typical pattern is to partition capacity: reserved pool for interactive, separate scheduled pool for batch, with cross-pool burst allowed if interactive lanes are underutilized. scheduling batch to off-peak windows and using preemption policies avoids contention.
[10:53] Claire: OK, curious about concrete numbers again: if we keep 4 GPUs baseline and allow 6 warm burst, what's the expected p95 delta at peak?
[11:01] Priya: rough estimate: if your model and sequence lengths are similar to our profile and you use fp16 with micro-batching, p95 should remain under 400ms if warm burst is ready; if cold burst the p95 could spike to multiple seconds for the first few requests due to model load.
[11:17] Tom: what about using smaller quantized model variant during spikes to preserve latency?
[11:21] Priya: that's a valid strategy: have a lower-cost quantized variant pinned as fallback; Redwood's smart routing can direct overflow traffic there. you'll want to run evals to check quality drop.
[11:32] Aaron: are there tooling hooks we can use to simulate spikes ourselves?
[11:37] Priya: yes, we provide a loadgen harness and scripts to replay traffic with your prompt set. we can share a pakej in the repo.
[11:45] Maya: security question: when using private deployment with Redwood control plane, where do encryption keys live?
[11:51] Priya: keys live in your KMS/HSM; we integrate via KMS APIs. Redwood doesn't hold keys for private/on-prem. for hosted, keys can be customer-managed with Bring-Your-Own-Key.
[12:03] Tom: anything else on the quantization—like mixed-precision during peak?
[12:08] Priya: mixed precision switching mid-flight isn't common; instead we recommend model-variant routing: route to fp16 or int8 variants based on SLA. the runtime supports fast model swap and parallel hosting of variants.
[12:20] Jesse: we should talk about warm pool sizing heuristics: often set warm capacity to historical 95th spike magnitude minus baseline. for example, if historical 95th is 120 and baseline 60, warm pool = capacity for 60 qps extra. but you can shape it depending on cost appetite.
[12:40] Tom: will Redwood help design the autoscale thresholds? we don't want to guess.
[12:44] Priya: yes, we do that as part of onboarding: we'll analyze your histograms, propose queue thresholds, pre-warm sizing, and cooldown windows. we also provide runbooks for incident response.
[12:55] Claire: about node placement — can we reserve GPUs across AZs?
[12:59] Priya: yes, multi-AZ placement is supported and recommended for failover, but it slightly increases warm pool cost since capacity is spread.
[13:10] Aaron: any thoughts on spot or preemptible nodes for burst?
[13:14] Priya: spot instances are cost-effective for non-critical batch; we don't recommend them for interactive warm pools because of potential preemption. spot can be part of the cold burst layer.
[13:24] Tom: regarding observability, can we get token-level traces for debugging slow requests?
[13:29] Priya: yes, we provide per-request traces including token timings, KV cache hits, kernel selection logs. they are viewable in Redwood Console and exportable.
[13:40] Jesse: it's probably a good place to pause; any remaining blockers?
[13:45] Tom: just need the pricing and the bench.
[13:48] Jesse: cool. recap of next steps: we'll send Dedicated pricing + burst policy doc, include a sample sizing calc, and a loadgen harness; you send traffic histograms and sample prompts; then we'll schedule bench.
[13:58] Priya: I'll also attach a short whiteboard doc on queueing models and a checklist for pre-warming KV cache.
[14:06] Maya: thanks, this was helpful.
[14:09] Aaron: thanks all.
[14:12] Jesse: thanks everyone, we will follow up by Friday with docs.
